ADVISORY COMMITTEE TO STUDY CURTAILMENT OF ELECTION EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several months ago
the government announced its intention to establish a committee to study election expenditures. This is a complex problem which affects the very basis of our democratic system. Moreover, it has become particularly important these last few years due to the increase of communication media, especially since the advent of television. It is now essential to take appropriate action so as to restrict and control election expenditures.
{Text]
Before proposing such measures, however, the government has decided to ask a small group of men with practical experience and expert knowledge to make a study of the problem of rising election expenses and make recommendations in the light of our own Canadian requirements and of the experience in other countries. The advisory committee will "inquire into and report upon the desirable and practical measures to limit and control federal election expenditures". These terms of reference are general, and we expect that the committee will give them a broad interpretation.
The members of the committee will be Mr. Frangois Nobert, Three Rivers, president; Hon. M. J. Coldwell, P.C., Ottawa; Mr. Gordon Dryden, Toronto; Mr. Arthur R. Smith, Calgary and Professor Norman M. Ward, Saskatoon.
We are very grateful to all these gentlemen for their willingness to serve on the committee. When their report is completed it will, of course, be made public. It is the first time in our country that a study of this kind has been undertaken and that a government has declared its intention to take effective steps to limit election expenditures. As a result of those steps we hope that our political
life will be improved and will reflect more faithfully our democratic ideals.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ADVISORY COMMITTEE TO STUDY CURTAILMENT OF ELECTION EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally I had no advance knowledge that this announcement would be made; therefore I shall not go into any detail, except to say the object is one that will commend itself not only to members of the house and defeated candidates but also to the public as a whole. Certainly the trend in recent years, resulting from television and radio and other necessary media of information, has brought about such an increase in constituency and election expenditures that it renders it very difficult for an average Canadian to take his part in public life.
When I mention expenditures I think of an election in Montreal, I believe it was in 1925 or 1926 in one of the constituencies in your city, sir, when the expenditures set out in the election returns by the two candidates involved were between $80,000 and $90,000 each. That was before the days of radio and television. All were legitimate expenditures; none the less the story is indicative of a great danger that democracy faces, namely that parliament shall be a place only for those who are able to supply the necessary funds. This is a particular detriment to young men and women desiring to take their part in public life.
So far as the personnel of the committee is concerned I commend the minister. I think all of them, both individually and collectively, are recognized by Canadians as a whole as having the necessary capacity and ability to face this difficult problem.

maintopic: ADVISORY COMMITTEE TO STUDY CURTAILMENT OF ELECTION EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the Secretary of State and the government for the step just announced. It seems to me this is the very heart of the whole question of democratic government. If we come to the day when elections can be bought and can be won by parties which have large campaign funds, then we will have lost a very vital element in our democracy. We all know that elections cost a great deal more than they used to, particularly if you have to pay for truth squads and pigeons-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ADVISORY COMMITTEE TO STUDY CURTAILMENT OF ELECTION EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
-and comic books. An investigation of the whole question of election expenses, of what measures can be taken to curtail them, and I hope also disclosure of the sources of campaign funds, would be an extremely useful thing if we are to develop democratic government in this country.
The government has taken the first step toward what we ought to have in Canada, a democratic system in which members will be elected to parliament on the basis of their merit and not on the basis of the gimmicks they can afford at election time.

maintopic: ADVISORY COMMITTEE TO STUDY CURTAILMENT OF ELECTION EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party join in welcoming the announcement that has been made by the Secretary of State. We all know that for a considerable length of time efforts have been made to spur action in this regard. We only hope the deliberations and studies of the committee will be conducted with dispatch so that before long we will have concrete suggestions and	recommendations
placed before the house.

maintopic: ADVISORY COMMITTEE TO STUDY CURTAILMENT OF ELECTION EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened carefully to the statement made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) to the effect that a committee will be formed to study the possibilities of decreasing election expenditures as much as possible.
If the work of this committee is directed with a view to allowing less wealthy candidates the opportunity to conduct an election campaign, then it will certainly be effective and will truly recognize the democratic principles which must prevail in a country like Canada.
Too often in the past we have deplored abuses during elections, and particularly during the last general election.
This study, Mr. Speaker, will not prevent the finance barons from supplying considerable amounts of money to the party in power and also to the official opposition party, which has always been done in the past. In many cases those large amounts have prevented able and serious persons from running, because they could not meet the extravagant expenditures of the major political parties of this country.
When some persons use, for instance, social legislation, family allowances, old age pensions, pensions for needy mothers, pensions for invalids, crippled and blind persons, under


the pretext that those social security measures were granted to them by the party in power, then they lie deliberately and shamelessly to the people of Canada, and the same applies as concerns agricultural subsidies.
Parliament as a whole, and not just a particular party, is responsible for social security legislation.
Mr. Speaker, we accept the statement of the Secretary of State when he tells us that the chairman of the committee concerned is a well-known Liberal of the province of Quebec, and we hope that this study will enable those who wish to run for office to face up to the candidates who benefit from considerable amounts supplied by barons of finance.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, before the house rose, last night, I said that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) likes to refer to the prosperity we are supposed to have in Canada at the present time. As late as this afternoon, he mentioned the prosperity of the automobile industry in Canada. It seems to have become typical of the Minister of Finance to talk about the present prosperity of the Canadian economy.
However, there is one thing he overlooks. He does not tell us for whom there is prosperity in Canada at the present time. There is probably prosperity for tax collectors and gatherers. Indeed, that field is in fact prosperous. Collections are much larger than before. Taxes have gone up and so, the coffers of the government are better lined than ever. [Text]

speechtext: Order. May I bring to the attention of members of the committee the fact that it is rather noisy. In fairness to hon. members who are trying to listen to the speech may I suggest that conversation should be carried on sotto voce.

speechtext: The hon. member for Lapointe has been speaking for a few minutes on a subject which appears to have no relation whatever with the subject under consideration, and I would invite him to come back to our discussion.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that during a debate on interim supply it has always been customary for the chairman to leave the greatest freedom to the members. As a feeling of revolt and fear seems to prevail today among Liberal members, this surely constitutes a matter of current interest.
I was saying that prosperity, to which the Minister of Finance refers so often, is a tax collector's prosperity; it is a national revenue department prosperity.
But look at the people, look at the unemployed, the farmer, the labourer, the small businessman, the small manufacturer. They are not prosperous. Prosperity is found among tax collectors, not among the people.
The surplus of which the Minister of Finance boasts at the present time does not imply a period of prosperity but a period of tax increases.
I said yesterday that unemployment statistics indicate a momentary improvement only because they are inaccurate. Nowadays, for instance, only those who get unemployment insurance benefits are considered as unemployed. However, there are just as many Canadians who are no longer entitled to such benefits, but who are covered by social insurance. Those people are still unemployed, but they are not classified as such because they do not draw unemployment insurance benefits.

Interim Supply
The situation is the same as in 1960, 1961, 1962 and 1963. The lot of the big fellows is improving but that of the little man is getting worse all the time.
What is the government doing in the circumstances? What legislation has this parliament passed to remedy Canada's present economic conditions?
According to orders of the day, 78 government orders have been put on the order paper during this session.
If you refer to order paper No. 177 for Tuesday, October 27, 1964, you will see that 52 of those government orders have been adopted by parliament. Among those 52, 14 were simply referred to a committee; therefore, nothing was solved, since those questions were referred to a committee for study.
There remain 38 orders, five of which dealt with supply or the estimates. In other words, this meant a two day debate which was nothing more than chatter, followed by a non-confidence motion at the end of those two days.
There remain 33. Five were also adopted on motions of approval of special measures which did not benefit the Canadian people. Among those five motions respecting special measures, there was the motion approving the sending of peace troops to Cyprus, a motion amending the constitution, that is, an address sent to the British parliament requesting the right to amend our constitution respecting old age pensions. There was also an address to the Queen of England after her trip to Canada.
All these motions concerning special bills have contributed absolutely nothing to the improvement of the economic situation in Canada.
So, we are left with 28 orders on the order paper which have been adopted by parliament.
Out of that number there were eight bills ordinarily called supply bills, four for interim supply and four for the supplementary estimates. The Canadian people did not get anything out of those either.
So we now have 20 bills which have been adopted by parliament. Out of that number, six were private bills and of minor importance from which the Canadian people did not get anything either. I might mention, for instance, the Blue Water Bridge Authority Act, the Judges Act and the Exchequer Court Act-simply to increase the number of judges-the Ste Foy-St. Nicolas Bridge Act and the Roosevelt Campobello International Park Commission Act.
[Mr. Grfegoire.l
Six such bills of very limited, special and secondary interest have been passed, with the result that there still remain but 14 bills, passed by parliament, which might have been of public interest.
Of those 14, three were based on budget resolutions brought forward when the Minister of Finance introduced his last budget. The sole purpose of those three bills was to increase taxes or change custom duties. Here again, the Canadian people did not get anything.
There are only 11 bills left which were passed by parliament, including five which merely served to amend other acts. One of them amended the National Defence Act, another the National Housing Act. Improvements brought to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could have been of benefit to the Canadian people if such advantages had not been completely nullified by the 11 per cent increase in the sales tax on building materials.
Of the six bills remaining, three concern agriculture and one the fishing zones. The only purpose of the three bills on agriculture was to run the Canadian people farther into debt: the first was to raise the amount of farm credit loans, the second to raise the amount of farm improvement loans and the third to extend credit to farm machinery syndicates.
Strangely enough, not one of those bills on agriculture is suitable to agriculture in eastern Canada.
There remains only two other bills passed by parliament this year; the first concerns a $10 family allowance to children aged 16 to 18 years, which will definitely not apply in the province of Quebec, since they are already getting it; the other, Bill No. C-lll, concerns $1,000 loans to students, which will not apply to the province of Quebec either.
There you have the legislative program put through by this government to date. Result: nil.
This means, Mr. Chairman, that the surplus now showing on government books results from taxes and not from the legislative program of the government.
The government did not legislate in the right direction. It was aiming at balancing a budget which had shown a deficit for the past eight or ten years. It legislated in the interest of the big financial interests of the country, not in the interest of the people.
But when England needs help to maintain the pound at its current level, then, the matter is urgent. There is no need to pass legisla-

tion. The Bank of Canada, without even explaining the circumstances to parliament or to the Canadian people, makes a low interest loan to the Bank of England.
When the British economy had to be saved, legislation was not even passed. The Bank of Canada did it without any act, without even consulting parliament, and it lent money practically free of interest to the Bank of England.
Since such a thing is possible to save the economic interests of England, why does the Bank of Canada not act in the same way in order to help the Canadian citizen, the individual, the small businessman? How can the Bank of Canada do that in order to help England, but cannot do the same thing to help our municipalities, school boards and provincial governments?
When the defence of big financial interests of English or international capitalists is involved, then there is no need for legislation. The Bank of Canada takes direct action, as it did less than three weeks ago, by lending tens of millions of dollars to England. But when the economic interests of the Canadian people are involved, there is nothing doing. As suggested by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), no legislation is introduced or our time is spent on passing legislation only to push people into debt, instead of pulling them out of the debt situation in which they are at the present time.
The Bank of Canada can act in the absence of legislation in order to save England's economy. Why could it not act now to save the economy of the Canadian people? Emergency measures are needed to save the Canadian economy at this time.
Demagogue.

Liberal members call that demagogy. One is asleep, the other one is reading his paper and there is another one who never did and never will understand anything. That is the contribution of certain Liberal members.
There was an emergency measure taken by the Bank of Canada to assist England and, in the same way, emergency measures must be applied in our country. Among those emergency measures, I should like to name four.
First, an emergency measure concerning every Canadian citizen. It involves three pieces of social security legislation to assist the individual where most needed.
The first step towards helping the individual would be to increase family allowances. The minister tells us that he has a
Interim Supply
surplus of $395 million. He should increase family allowances in order to give parents of large families, which number five, seven, eight and even ten children, the opportunity to send them to school, give them a decent and honourable life, and provide clothing, food and shelter for them during their studies. We should raise family allowances to $10, $18, or $20 per month in order that those children might attend school-not only primary school, but also secondary school or even university. It is the duty of the government to raise family allowances for all the young people of our country, so that everyone may take advantage of our educational facilities.
A second measure would involve old age pensions. Look at what is going on in the factories today. Come and see for yourselves what is taking place in the big factories in my riding, such as the Aluminum Company in Arvida and Price Brothers in Kenogami and Jonquiere. You will see that the worker is retired at 65 years of age. While he is used to a decent salary, he must, at age 65 be retired on a pension that is not enough for him to live on.
As industry and factory workers retire at 65, it seems to me that the government should lower to 65 the age for old age pensions, instead of keeping it at 70. The monthly pension of $75 should be paid to all Canadian citizens 65 years of age, because nowadays factory workers are increasingly being retired at that age and are deprived of their salary, not at 70 but at 65 years of age.
The third point concerns social security. Today we notice that one of the greatest problems faced by the individual and the big family-I know that there is hospital insurance to pay for a public ward-comes from doctors' and anaesthetists' bills, and the price of medicine and operations. The government should pass legislation as quickly as possible with a view to organizing a system of health dividend, in the form of dividend coupons which would be sent to all family heads and to all single people over 21 years of age. Each head of a family and each single person could use these dividend coupons to subscribe to a medical care program with an insurance company of his choice, whether profit-making or not.
Private insurance companies in Canada are in a position to offer health insurance plans, and this would be an economy for the government. A greater number of Canadian citizens would be insured through this health dividend which would only be valid with a Canadian company.

Interim Supply
Then the Canadian citizen would be in a position to pay his expenses not only for hospitalization in a public ward but also for a private room, when necessary, as well as the fees of physicians, surgeons, anaethetists and expenses for drugs, house calls and so on.
Those three measures, that is family allowances, old age pensions and health dividends would directly help the individual to live better under our present system.
The first point, the first piece of urgent legislation which should be enacted in Canada is a social security bill concerning family allowances, old age pensions at the age of 65 and a universal health dividend.

Here then, Mr. Chairman, is the second measure, and I shall refer to it very briefly.
It would be to provide work for each and every Canadian citizen. There are too many unemployed at the present time in our country, whether or not they are included in the statistics. By carrying out a vast program of public works, improving our public buildings, our roads, our bridges, building schools and universities and also looking after urban renewal, we should be able, by means of such a vast program of public works, to provide jobs for all our Canadian citizens.

The third emergency measure essential to Canada is to find the solution to the problem of agriculture in eastern Canada. At the present time, agriculture in eastern Canada is in complete stagnation. Its reactivation would require emergency measures, and to these we would be ready to contribute. By so doing, we could save the farmer in eastern Canada, and especially in the province of Quebec, from ruination and bankruptcy.
The fourth emergency measure would be to reduce taxes so that the Canadian government would not take away from the Canadian citizen the salary he earns, as is done through taxes at the present time.
Let the government bring forward those four urgent measures and then, we are convinced, prosperity will follow, not a false or artificial prosperity that benefits tax collectors but prosperity for each and every Canadian citizen. It is the responsibility of all members of this house to promote the prosperity of all Canadian citizens and not only that of tax collectors.

Once before in another nation, now our ally, a man with views like Rockwell came to power unnoticed by forces that might have stopped him. By the time his nation was aware of the threat he posed, it was too late for he was already in firm control and could not be stopped.

This is the statement that preceded the television program in which Rockwell was pictured as the commander of the American nazi party, with a huge flag bearing the swastika, and bordered by some 20 or 30 stalwarts, strong-arm men. Where, in the opinion of a representative of the board, a promotional program broadcast by a station is of an offensive or objectionable nature, or is likely to create or contribute to any public disturbance or disorder, that representative may, by notice in writing, require that station to show cause, in the manner and within the time indicated in the notice, why the character of that program should not be modified.

Rockwell vilified Dr. Martin Luther King. I will not dignify his statement by repeating

No station or network operator shall broadcast-
(b) any abusive comment or abusive pictorial representation on any race, religion or creed-
I do not see how the C.B.C. can clear themselves of the implication of the violation of this article. One of the co-producers of the program is quoted in the Toronto Star for October 26, 1964 as having said this. The co-producer's name is Douglas Leiterman, who explained:

Therefore I submit, Mr. Chairman, that responsible people do not make irresponsible statements, and that irresponsible people should be held responsible for irresponsible statements. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something about the C.B.C. along a somewhat different line than that followed by most of those who have spoken so far, whose remarks have been related chiefly to programming. In my view the complaints in this regard are the result of the organization of the C.B.C., the manner in which it carries on its operations and the lack of any real control over these operations by anybody.
As we all know, the C.B.C. is not accountable to the government or to any cabinet

minister for its operations. Theoretically control can be exercised by parliament itself. In actual fact parliament has been very loath to exercise that control. From the practical point of view the only way parliament can exercise any control is, first, by withholding funds for the operation of the C.B.C., something we have not been prepared to do largely because there is insufficient information available as to the amount which should be withheld and the purpose for which it should be withheld.
The second way in which control can be exercised is by the appointment of a committee of the house to look into the affairs of the C.B.C. There is no standing committee of the house on broadcasting, and special committees have been set up at relatively infrequent intervals. As a result they have not served as an effective means for parliament to exercise control over the C.B.C.
I think a great improvement could be made in this regard if a standing committee on broadcasting were set up and divided into subcommittees, each of which could pursue in detail the operations of a particular phase of the C.B.C.'s activities and thus be able to arrive at an appraisal of what was going on, with the result that the committee would be in a position to make specific recommendations as to the improvements which should be made and as to the course which should be followed.
More important even than the fact that parliament has had no practical means of controlling the C.B.C.'s expenditures or its operations is that it has had no means even of ensuring that the views and recommendations of the committees it has appointed are implemented. In many cases the C.B.C. has paid no attention whatever to the views which have been expressed in these committees and in this chamber itself. A good example of how little attention the C.B.C. pays to the only body to which theoretically it is accountable is the fact that there is no one here in the official gallery from the C.B.C. today paying any attention to the debate which is now taking place; and I doubt whether there is anybody from the C.B.C. in any of the galleries. In other words, what they say is "We don't care what parliament says about us. We don't care what parliament wants. We are going to run our show in the way we want and parliament can go ahead and talk as much as it likes; it will not affect us."

A little later in my remarks I intend to deal briefly with matters concerning the C.B.C. Perhaps the committee would be patient for a while because, being an Irishman, it takes me a little while to get to the point.
As I said a few moments ago, I cannot discuss separatism with the detailed knowledge of a Mason Wade, nor can I lay claim to the title of a political scientist, nor have I majored in Canadian history. I can only discuss separatism and its effect on Quebec and on Canada, from the insight that 43 years of happy existence in Quebec has given me-43 years as part of a minority within a minority; 43 years in which I was never conscious until very recently that perhaps, as an Anglo-Saxon, I was not entirely welcome in the province of my birth.
I have mentioned before in this house, in glowing terms I might add, my feelings of respect and affection for the French Canadians with whom I have been privileged to live for so long. But I would be betraying that friendship and, indeed, insulting these same people if I did not stand here and say there have been many changes in Quebec. These changes, in many cases, are for the better-I have in mind the progress made in the fields of education and economics, for example. But one change I have not relished particularly has been the tendency of many of our political leaders to introduce racism into their political philosophies. Perhaps political instincts are such that it is not exactly wise for an English speaking person living in the province of Quebec to discuss separatism, particularly one who numbers French speaking Canadians among the majority of his electors. Then again, none of us

was elected to this house to perpetuate his role as parliamentarian. All of us were elected to speak out on matters of importance affecting the unity of this country. It is in this light that I should like to discuss separatism and somewhere along the line tie these remarks in with the administrative problems of Canada.
There are misguided optimists, Mr. Chairman, who view the fact that bodily harm did not come to the Queen as an indication that separatism is limited to a few misguided youths, badly organized, a group that will disappear of its own volition. There are others who are very pessimistic because of the deplorable events that marked the Queen's visit to Quebec, people who see separatists behind every tree, people who feel that separatism is lurking around the corner, and who in their panic, judge every action, every word of the French speaking Canadian leaders with suspicion and mistrust. The truth, of course, Mr. Chairman, is that the separatist problem is much more serious than these optimists realize, but not nearly as insoluble as the prophets of doom would have us believe.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that it is in our best interests to analyse the make up of this movement, for only in understanding the motivation behind its leaders and its members will we be able to suggest the required solutions or decide upon a course of action. Perhaps the one fact that English speaking Canada does not understand, Mr. Chairman, is that the hard core of the separatist movement does contain many sincere people who fully believe in the separatist cause. Never mind whether they are misguided, according to our beliefs; what is more important is to realize that these people do not espouse violence. They do not necessarily hate the English. They simply believe that a new state of Quebec, independent of the rest of Canada, is the best solution for the frustrations and nationalistic feelings of many of their followers. They believe that a separate state will lead to unlimited opportunities for the expansion of their culture, to unlimited job opportunities, to a type of Utopia that seems very rational for those who are blinded by their devotion to a cause. But we must bear in mind, Mr. Chairman, that these people, misguided as they may be, are entitled to their opinion, entitled to their movement, precisely in the same way as we provide freedom of expression for those who espouse liberalism, conservatism, socialism or even communism.

But unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, this hard core of idealists has attracted, as indeed all such movements do attract, a lunatic fringe. These misfits are made up of neurotics, of people who would be failures in any society, including, I might add, a new state of Quebec, if the movement were successful. They include those who revel in the false security of publicity, who delight in the prominence that their acts of violence provides them. They see in the separatist movement, not an ideal, not a dream, but rather a means to a degree of personal recognition which normally would be denied them because of their insignificant contribution to Quebec society.
The movement is made even more dangerous by the very fact that it has invaded our universities, that our young people, at the very moment that they are being introduced to the philosophies of great men, of Locke, and Montesquieu, of Aristotle and St. Thomas Aquinas, are being exposed to morbid separatist tendencies. At the very time when we look to the new emphasis on education in Quebec, to produce the leaders of the future, our young men and young women are being filled with the inward-looking theories of pseudo-intellectuals, who by their message of hatred and misunderstanding are prostituting their role as educators, are poisoning whole generations of young French speaking Canadians. And finally, Mr. Chairman, add to this collection those political leaders, those leaders in the field of communications, of radio, of television, those in the journalistic world, who take advantage of the movement to bolster sagging reputations, to gain some shortsighted political advantage, to seek the power that to too many politicians is the prime goal of their very existence.
Perhaps I sound like the pessimists to whom I referred earlier in my remarks. I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that I felt precisely that way several months ago; I felt, then, that the apathy of Canadians outside this house to the question of separatism would in the end permit its growth to a point of no return. To generalize is very dangerous, but surely the efforts of some of our daily newspapers from outside Quebec have provided the very publicity upon which the lunatic fringe breeds. Not too long ago, Mr. Chairman, I bought a daily newspaper published in Ontario. Three quarters of the front page was devoted to an exclusive interview with a separatist who predicted violence to the Queen. He spoke of the movement of arms

Ten months ago, Mr. Chairman, I thought we would lose the battle, by default, for these people's minds. I realized, as no doubt many hon. members have realized, that the separatist movement had so far been confined to certain intellectuals, to young students, and to what I have already referred to as the lunatic fringe. I realized that the very acts of violence that were the responsibility of this lunatic fringe were in fact offsetting amongst the uncommitted the admitted emotional appeal of nationalism. Perhaps the extremist wing of the separatist movement did not realize, or perhaps did not care, that their acts of violence, their intemperate statements, were only impeding the message of the sincere, if misguided, nucleus who really believe in their movement and who hope to achieve it by democratic means.

We can thank the Lord, Mr. Chairman, that we cannot obliterate history; for what a tremendous price French Canada would be called upon to pay. Surely, Mr. Chairman, the right of French speaking Canadians to their proper place in the nation's affairs must be clear not only to those separatists but also to those all too numerous persons who refuse to accept fully the French fact across Canada.
I had hoped for one voice or more to express these views; for one politician to talk back, to explode the myths of Anglo-Saxon domination in Quebec, to lay the blame for some of Quebec's lack of economic growth squarely on the shoulders of the inwardlooking policies of Mr. Duplessis. But the pendulum of separatism seemed to stop and the voices of reason did seem to speak back. On May 14 seven French Canadian intellectuals of international repute published what is known as a Canadian manifesto. It is significant that they called it a Canadian manifesto and not a Quebec manifesto. They published this historical document in a magazine known as Cite Libre, a magazine that led the way in Quebec for the emergence of freedom of thought and freedom of expression that was denied the intellectuals of Quebec by Mr. Duplessis. This document exposed separatism

for what it is, an escape from reality, a move that would do nothing for French Canada but would relegate it from a strong, respected voice in Canada to a voice drowned out by the sheer numbers of a completely English speaking continent.
The question of separatism must be faced, and faced immediately. Those intellectuals of Quebec who espouse separatism must be challenged by those intellectuals of Quebec who espouse federalism. Our politicians must speak up; our students must be exposed to the fallacy of the separatist movement.
Several people in this house, Mr. Chairman, are doing precisely that. The Secretary of State's speeches six months or a year ago were treated with scorn in my province. Today they are being reviewed and reviewed again by those who are seeking ways out of our problems. The assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce has shown willingness to do verbal battle in Quebec on the question of separatism. The hon. member for Three Rivers has obviously been making a contribution, as recent events testify. The views of moderation expressed by the hon. member for Villeneuve a few weeks ago did much to reassure the people of this country of the sincerity, maturity and integrity of our Quebec politicians. Recent articles in Le Devoir, he Droit, Le Soleil and L'Action all indicate that those who believe in federalism have many strong and vigorous allies in Quebec, allies who could mean the difference between a nation united and reaching out toward its great destiny or a nation so divided by petty quarrels that it must pale into insignificance and eventually disappear.
While I rejoice at the appearance of cracks in the armour of separatism I cannot but wonder what will happen when the separatist movement virtually disappears, as it will, by the efforts of the French speaking Quebeckers who once again will show the realism that has marked their fight for survival as a cultural group. What will happen, Mr. Chairman, to the separatists outside Quebec when our French speaking Canadians turn once again to Ottawa; when they express a desire once again to participate in the nation's business? Will the doors be closed to them in industry outside Quebec? Will they be expected to forget their own language and every day affairs? Can they look for some relief from the oppressive legislation which in many provinces denies them the rights to which they are entitled under the British North America Act? I refer to rights in the field of education, and education in their own language; rights which

I have always enjoyed as an Anglo-Saxon in the province of Quebec.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, the appearance of Rockwell on the C.B.C. was not such a bad thing after all, for it emphasized in a vivid, incisive manner that we have no room in this country for hatred and racism. This obviously sick individual showed us the results of racism and provided us with some food for thought in this country of ours.
Those political leaders in Canada who introduce racism in their arguments-and make no mistake there are many-are either intentionally or unintentionally creating an atmosphere which leads to the type of hatred personified by Rockwell. What is the difference between Rockwell's contempt for the negro and those misguided Canadians who contemptuously tell French speaking people to speak the white man's language? What is the difference between Rockwell's evil, disgusting remarks concerning those of the Jewish faith and the utterances of those who condemn the French speaking people because of their religious beliefs? On that latter point, let me say that I have in my possession many articles on this very subject which have been written in well accepted magazines which are circulated in this country.
Let me say this: Our country will stand out like a jewel among nations by reason of our two cultures. They are cultures which do not detract from each other but which, by their contrast, emphasize the greatness of each. This is the dream we should all be striving for, the good life so ably outlined in the Canadian manifesto, required reading, I suggest, for all of us who are vitally concerned with national unity.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I say that I am sure of the disappearance of the French speaking separatist. Can anyone in this house guarantee me the disappearance of the English speaking separatist?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Verdun on his wise, reasoned, reasonable, very sound and very eloquent remarks which he has addressed to a profoundly important subject. In the manner of his delivery he demonstrated that he is indeed gifted, as are most Irish folk, with great felicity of phrase and it was a pleasure to hear him. I remember his leader, the Prime Minister, saying some months ago, when the hon. member for Three Rivers spoke eloquently in French on a similar subject, that the voice of moderation and reason must be heard in this house and in this country both
Interim Supply
in English and in French. I think today, Mr. Chairman, we have heard in English a most sound and valuable discourse on the subject to which we all must give our very best not only of attention but of effort.
If I were not a Scotsman, Mr. Chairman,
I would probably carry on with the subject raised by the hon. member, who said he took a long time to get started. But being a Scot I am stubborn and I think I will continue with the subject I had in my mind before the hon. member made his speech. The question of the C.B.C., as with questions concerning all our crown corporations, is an extremely difficult one. On Friday the hon. member for Port Arthur discussed the question of control in connection with the railway. The hon. member for Calgary North in his very wise and valuable speech dealt with the same subject and the relationship between parliament and crown corporations. I know it is very easy for the Secretary of State or the Minister of National Revenue, almost as a conditioned response, to say they will transmit so and so's views to the management of the C.B.C. This has been the practice for a long time. Yet as representatives of the public we cannot divorce ourselves from our concern for this tremendously important medium.
In a very valuable document, the Massey royal commission on arts, letters and sciences, I find in the section dealing with broadcasting at page 276 of the report a most interesting elucidation of this very question.
The state, having the right and the duty of issuing licences, must impose certain conditions on radio broadcasting. There are, it seems to us, two alternative views between which every country must choose. First, radio may be regarded primarily as a means of entertainment, a by-product of the advertising business. Such a view does not imply that it may not be used for education, for enlightenment and for the cultivation of taste; all these bring entertainment to many people. On the other hand, radio, as one of the most powerful means of education, may be regarded as a social influence too potent and too perilous to be ignored by the state which, in modern times, increasingly has assumed responsibility for the welfare of its citizens.
This welfare, of course, extends beyond the provision of food, clothing and shelter.
I am not going to join in any vendetta against the C.B.C. It is not my purpose in the few minutes allowed me to put that institution in the dock and fire verbal arrows at it. I would not want this country without the C.B.C. It is one of the things I miss most when I happen to be abroad. Nor would it be useful to me to indulge in discussing my tastes and preferences as to what should be heard over the C.B.C. or aired over C.B.C.

Interim Supply
television. The old Latin expression, de gustibus non est disputandum, applies or, as they say in French, chacun a son gout. I suppose I have just demonstrated to you, Mr. Chairman, that I am a little worse in French than I am in Latin. But there is no accounting for human tastes, and we could all discuss at great length that which we like and that which we do not like.
What I am concerned about is that we seem to be in one of those phases where there is a widespread feeling of concern and anxiety about the C.B.C. among the public. This is not just something that has sprung up because of a program last Sunday night. We find all sorts of people and organizations taking aim at this time at the C.B.C. and it is not enough to reply that they are independent in management and independent in administration and so on.
I know it is a dangerous course to come even close to suggesting that points of view, however unpleasant, should be muffled, that some sort of censor should be appointed, because the question then is: How do you trust the censor and whom do you trust to become censor? Yet there is a very definite reason for people today asking, as hon. members have asked this afternoon, why we hear so often, so frequently, from the fanatics, the extremists, the oddballs.
We must be realistic and admit that sensationalism is seemingly the most valuable ingredient of reportorial journalism. There have been a lot of good speeches made today, a lot of good speeches were made yesterday and there will be a lot of good speeches made tomorrow, but the people of Canada will not hear too much about them. As a member of the house once said, if he made a good speech it might be reported on page 17 of some newspaper but if he stood on his head it would be flashed on the front page. This session has been so long, and even a young man like myself is so tired, that I would not dare try to do that because if I ever got inverted I might not get converted. But this is a fact that we must face.
It is unfortunate that there seems to be such a plethora of the off-colour, of the fantastic, of the "way-out". I thought today, as the Secretary of State was announcing the names of the members of his commission on election expenses, and a very illustrious group of names they were, of how much it would cost any of us as candidates to get the prime time that the leader of the American nazi party got over C.B.C. television.

I would hope I will always be able to admit the need, indeed the desirability of airing stimulating ideas, even if they are disturbing to me and unpopular to the majority. In a country like ours we require a free market of ideas but in that market let there be some ample stalls for the stable and even the staid elements of our society. Let us hear more often the voices of those who cherish our contemporary political and social institutions. Let us give the platform more often to those who desire not to tear down but to shore up the bulwarks of the society to which we belong.
It is difficult to avoid the impression that mere appearance on a publicly owned television or radio network lends some status, sanction or authority to the views that are aired through those facilities. This of course is wrong, and if we have a moment to apply our rational processes we know it is wrong. In connection with the seemingly famous program of last Sunday night I commend the C.B.C. for their efforts to set the stage for that dreadful racist from the United States and to disavow in advance his evil utterances. However, while I have a high regard for the credibility of people I am afraid that not all viewers and listeners got the full import of the C.B.C.'s very proper disavowal and disengagement.
We only have to remember what happened a few years ago when Orson Welles' famous program, "The War of the Worlds", was aired over radio in the United States. Although not once but thrice it was clearly laid out that this was fantasy, that this was a drama, that it was not true, hundreds of people ran outside their homes fearful that missiles from outer space were going to crash upon them. This is one of the facts we must face.
Since we seem anxious to talk about this program-I might say this was the first time I had seen it-I think that while it is perhaps not a large matter the C.B.C. did commit an impropriety or an act of unneighbourliness in releasing a political film prepared for viewers in the United States which the leaders of the party in the United States who ordered the production of the film decided should not be seen. Our own Canada Elections Act, for instance, would prohibit any of us from using United States television facilities to beam in a program upon the voters in our own area. With a little careful thought I feel that the corporation would not have undertaken this sort of thing.

What do we do? Do we put the C.B.C. into shackles? Do we put it into receivership? Do we make it an agency of some government department? Do we put it under a minister?
I say no, no, a thousand times no. As much as I think of the Secretary of State I would not think it would be a proper move to put the C.B.C. under his wing or under the wing of any minister of any government, because this is the very kind of control that we do not want and must not have in a free democracy. You cannot have a government controlling the media with the media becoming an emanation of any particular set of thoughts. We do not want thought control. Yet the canons of good taste, good judgment and administrative economy must remain operative. They must emanate from somewhere. They must be directed by someone.
Like the hon. member for Calgary North I am concerned about the apparent insensitivity of the C.B.C. president and management to the views of the public. No one would suggest that the C.B.C. must run for shelter at every expression of public opinion and that it try to prejudge popular reaction and go always to the side of the majority. If the C.B.C. had done this through the years, and had not done that which was unpopular and unprofitable we would have much poorer radio and television fare in this country today. I will never join those who would destroy the C.B.C. or who would turn the whole thing over to private enterprise. I have lived in lands where all radio and television were in the beneficent hands of private businessmen and more than ever I thought that the C.B.C. was a pretty good thing. I do not think I am being un-Conservative in this regard because I recall the whole thing began in the days of a very great Canadian prime minister, R. B. Bennett.
You would never know it now.

Well, perhaps it is not as good as it was in the days of R. B. Bennett, but I do not have the time to go into value judgments of that kind. As we know the legislation certainly envisaged, as did that great prime minister, that it would be a vehicle for national education, for national unity. In this field it has grown to play an essential and valuable part in Canadian life. It is for this reason I am concerned and why I am taking a few minutes to enter this discussion.
The C.B.C. is such a valuable part of our life, so important to all of us in these days when there is such a plethora of idea coming

in upon men's minds. It is extremely important that the C.B.C. not endanger its effectiveness or diminish its usefulness in the country. I am fearful that it might lose its effectiveness, both potentially and actually, if it goes too far in its disregard for the deep-seated anxieties of many Canadians. I was impressed by the group of women's organizations read out by the hon. member for Medicine Hat yesterday. This is not a group of narrow-minded Mrs. Grundys looking for notoriety. These are respectable, reputable and highly intelligent people. I share, in sorrow and in sympathy, the closing sentence in this article:
How did the usually circumspect C.B.C. manage to alienate so many of those who should be its friends and supporters?
The C.B.C. does not have to win a popularity contest, but it cannot find itself in a position where the great bulk of Canadian people look upon it with distrust, suspicion and indeed with hostility. I believe that at this stage in its operation, and it is an important phase for it, the C.B.C. would benefit and Canada would benefit greatly from the establishment of such a committee as has been suggested by many hon. members. There are many known areas for administrative improvement. It is quite possible that many more would come to light. There are many suggestions which could be made. It is often alleged that there is a little too much centralization of thought in the C.B.C. We have very valuable public affairs programs with informed opinion from here and there. I do not belong to that great group of Canadians who believe that "hate Toronto" is a valuable motto. However, I do not see why so many of the informed people and ideas must emanate from Toronto. There are in other parts of the country people with ideas on contemporary problems from whom I should like to hear from time to time. In recent years I am happy that we have heard a great deal from informed, intelligent commentators in the province of Quebec whose major language is French. I hope that equal opportunity is given listeners on the French network to hear from the same type of people in the English speaking sector of our society.
There are things which we should look into. I was shocked yesterday to hear that a member of the Quebec cabinet suggested the C.B.C. was suffering from communist infiltration. The television reporters for the C.B.C. French network, I understand, have protested the statement by Hon. Bona Arsenault that the network was the scene of left wing

Interim Supply
communist infiltration. I feel that this is a very serious allegation. I hope it is not true. Until I am convinced otherwise, I believe it is not true. This is another proper field for a sane, calm, cool investigation, followed by suggestions from a parliamentary committee. I would urge the setting up of such a committee. No one wants an outbreak of anxiety, reaching crisis proportions, about the C.B.C. We do not want this to become yet another trouble in the country which is allowed to develop into massive proportions. Then, to be followed by serious adjustments and retreats. Let us deal with it now. There has been a widespread expression of opinion, so let a move be taken and have the matter looked at by a committee.
It will not help Canada, it will not help any of us, if the C.B.C. is degraded and its effectiveness diminished. Let us move now. I join in support of those who have suggested the efficacy of a committee, not a witch hunting committee but a committee which will seek ways of improving the effectiveness of the C.B.C. or, to use a favourite expression, improving the image of the C.B.C., which is so valuable to all of us. None of us wants to see it reach a point where it is going to lose its great value in our society.

Mr. Chairman, I would have been quite happy to leave any remarks I had to make about the C.B.C. until the estimates of that department were before us. Apparently, however, we are going to have interim supply for some time, the subject is up for discussion, so I am getting in at this particular point. I want to make my remarks about the general criticisms which have been made, and then later I have some particular remarks concerning the selection of the C.B.C. site in Vancouver.
The hon. member for Calgary North, speaking earlier, referred to the relationship of the British Broadcasting Corporation and the British parliament. He thought that was a good type of relationship and perhaps one that we should have here. I quite agree. I would remind hon. members that in the United Kingdom parliament, members are not up every day during the question period sniping away at the B.B.C. or asking questions about the programs. There is a properly established committee which periodically reviews the complete operations of the British Broadcasting Corporation and I believe also of the independent television networks which have been set up in recent years. It seems to me that much of the discussion which we have 
had here in the last few months has been out of order. It would have been much better to have discussed these matters at the time the estimates were before us. We will have a further opportunity when the committee, headed by Mr. Fowler, reports in a few months time. His committee is making a very thorough investigation of the broadcasting industry. I imagine this report will be the subject of intensive study by parliament itself and by a parliamentary committee.
There are many aspects of the C.B.C. operation, Mr. Chairman, which properly should concern members of parliament. They should be concerned about the operational budget of the corporation and about the building budget. We have heard a great deal about the sum of money that is being spent on buildings in Toronto and Montreal. Perhaps this is too much. We should be concerned, I think, about the lack of decentralization of the operations of the C.B.C. and the tremendous concentrations in Toronto and Montreal. All of these things should be of concern at the proper time.
One thing we should not be concerned about, as was stated by some hon. members yesterday, notably the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan), is the daily programming of the corporation. To show how ridiculous we might get I want to read briefly from an editorial which appeared in the Peterborough Examiner last spring at the time of the "Open Grave" controversy.
We can imagine what would happen if the C.B.C. was directly responsible to parliament, instead of through its president and a minister of the crown. The Commons would hardly have time for any other business, so eager are its members to be broadcasting experts. The result might well be live programs from the Commons itself: "Mr. Speaker, ladies and gentlemen of our television audience, I am the Conservative member from Brassneck and the Islands and am about to give the government a severe drubbing..." What fun the public could have switching channels and corrupting itself with American programs while this was going on!
The type of activity that is being carried on in this chamber concerning programming was well described last April in the television column of the Globe and Mail written by Dennis Braithwaite in which he said:
A case could be made for a full investigation of broadcasting (its public and private segments and the B.B.G.-not just the C.B.C.) and the corporation itself has asked for such an inquiry. What is not needed is another witch hunt in which the C.B.C. is asked to account for every hell and damn spoken by its actors, every unpopular or even scandalous opinion expressed by its commentators and every inch of leg shown by its dancers.

Most of all, let's not have a big hullabaloo about bringing the C.B.C. under the control of parliament. It must be made clear somehow, to backbenchers and to crusaders like Mr. Hogan that the C.B.C., although responsible to parliament in the ultimate sense, has always been and must continue to be entirely free to run its business under its mandate.
I agree that there is some clarification needed concerning its mandate. Perhaps something along the lines of the B.B.C. is what we need, but I am quite prepared to wait until the Fowler committee makes its report before dealing with that theory.
I was quite disturbed yesterday by some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Northwest Territories. He named a number of programs which appeared in the "Quest" and "Festival" series, and used such terms as "filth," "homosexuality" and "pornography." In fact he used these terms fairly frequently. I do not know what kind of authority the hon. member is on filth, pornography, homosexuality and other subjects.
I do not know who is an authority on these matters. However I suggest that the average member of parliament is probably not a very good drama critic, and I further suggest not many programs that appear on the C.B.C. deal with these controversial subjects.
I do not think anyone would dispute the fact that the broadcasting medium from time to time ought to deal with controversial subjects.

My point is that most of the time on the C.B.C. television network is taken up with pretty standard broadcasting fare, and there is very little in this controversial field. Most of it comes up in drama broadcasts, but I submit that throughout the ages dramatists have brought in controversial material in order both to entertain and make the public think. Shakespeare did it, and any dramatist worthy of the name has done the same thing. There is not much real controversial drama presented on radio and television and I do not believe we should complain about the small amount that is broadcast.

We should continue to have that type of program, and if people are shocked now and then, what of it? You cannot please all the people all the time.
One person who is apparently quite highly regarded by our television audiences is Mr. Lome Greene, the star of the program "Bonanza." Years ago he lived in this country and got his start on the C.B.C. When he visited Montreal earlier this year he was interviewed, and I quote from the Montreal Star of March 31 last:
Lome Greene looked back proudly yesterday on his alma mater, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and spoke of its courage in maintaining its programming independence, as in the case of the controversial "Open Grave" program last week. Then, referring to U.S. television, which has made

him one of its stars, he said "this kind of courage is also becoming more frequent on the American networks, as we can see in such explosive programs as those on integration and other social and political conditions."
We have this type of exploratory, controversial program which arouses people and causes them to think. Mr. Greene suggests the Americans are now beginning to adopt the same idea, and I suggest this is something of which we should be proud.
Another Canadian actor who spends some of his time in the U.S., Mr. Lloyd Bochner, had this to say, and I quote from the Globe and Mail of March 13 last, at a time when he was back in Canada to do a program for the "Festival" series:
Few things they're doing in the United States can compare with the aspirations and standards of the Canadian t.v. scene these days. This role I'm doing now, for instance, is one of the toughest I can remember.
Mr. Bochner appears in many U.S. t.v. shows but they are usually of a very standard variety and he felt the "Festival" show was a challenge for him to develop a new acting role on the C.B.C.
My contention, Mr. Chairman, is that the amount of criticism we hear is not justified. Since yesterday's debate I conducted my own private poll among members of parliament. In fact I would like to know how much criticism is being directed to members from the public. I represent a constituency in the lower mainland of British Columbia. It is a riding which contains approximately 35,000 households, and since January 1, 1964 I have had one complaint about the C.B.C. Someone complained that a wrestling show on Saturday afternoon was cancelled. I checked with two other members from the lower mainland or greater Vancouver area, and neither had received complaints. I checked with three members from the Toronto area, the second most populous area in the country, and one admitted to having one complaint. I also checked with three members from the Montreal area and one of them admitted to having one complaint. I suggest that the widespread public criticism which is supposed to exist does not in fact exist and that members of parliament are not hearing from the Canadian people in any large numbers about the quality of the programs.
For my part I believe there is one other criticism which should be made in the field of telecasting in Canada. This is a subject to which I believe the Fowler committee could well direct its attention. I refer to the

difference between some of the promises made by certain private telecasters when they were applying for licences from the board of broadcast governors and their performance subsequently. In the October issue of the ACTRA Newsmagazine, the publication of the association of Canadian television and radio artists, appears the proceedings at the hearing of the board of broadcast governors when Mr. Bushnell was making an application for a television licence for CJOH-TV here in Ottawa. We are given a verbatim report of what he promised, side by side with comments upon what has been done. There were great promises made concerning the amount of money which would be spent on Canadian talent and Canadian shows. These promises have simply not materialized. In fact, ACTRA says, since the station began broadcasting in 1961, members of the association have earned $180 for performing. Nevertheless, thousands of dollars were promised for Canadian talent. As I say, I believe this subject is worthy of investigation, bearing in mind the fact that the C.B.C. does spend very large sums of money providing a living for entertainers and artists of many kinds and making it possible for them to work full time in their occupations, supplementing their income from other sources. Without work for the C.B.C. it would not be possible for them to do this.
If you got Doug Fisher in the organization it would probably cost more than it does now.

Well, he is quite a performer.
Mention has been made of the controversial program in the series "This Hour has Seven Days". I saw the second half of the program during which the American nazi Rockwell was interviewed. The hon. member for Cartier took strong exception to this broadcast and I realize his feelings on this subject may well be different from mine. I did not have the impression, as he apparently did, that it was simply sensationalism. The hon. member mentioned the fact that Rockwell stated there were about 100 members of his group in Canada. But I suggest that anti-Semitism does exist in this country, latently in some cases and openly in others, and that this is a proper subject for inquiry. There are other Americans with whom I do not agree, people for whom in fact I have no liking. But I would not object to their being interviewed on Canadian television. Most Canadians are interested in the United States political scene. There is one group known as the Black Muslims who do not like the white race generally. It could

well be that members of this organization would be interviewed in the United States even if they were not allowed to cross the border into Canada.
I think the interviewers on this particular program did a good job of exposing this man.
I can understand there are people who feel very sensitive about this and I realize their reactions could be very different from my own. But I do think this is the type of controversial, searching program the production needs and I imagine that if the producers do their work properly there will be a great many more complaints and a great deal more controversy in the future.
There is another aspect of this whole question of the continual sniping at C.B.C. programs, and this disturbs me. Even if the minister responsible does not actively interfere with programming-and he should not do so; indeed, I do not think he will-and even if the board of broadcast governors does not move against the corporation, I fear there will be a tendency on the part of management itself to listen to the large number of criticisms which have been made here and to begin to exercise some self-censorship. I know this is what the critics want, but I believe the corporation would be much the poorer if it were to take action along this line.
I wish now to deal with a matter of more local interest relating to the C.B.C. I am glad to see that the Postmaster General who himself comes from the city of Vancouver is present in the house because this has to do particularly with the C.B.C. in Vancouver. As you are aware, Mr. Chairman, there has been a controversy during the past few months between the Vancouver city council on the one hand and the corporation and the federal government on the other. The R.C.A.F. has given up certain facilities at Kitsilano park, Vancouver, and the parks board would like the whole site to revert completely to parkland. The C.B.C. wanted to take a small part of that site as a location for its studios during the next few years. At the present time the C.B.C. studios in Vancouver are scattered all over the downtown area. Radio facilities are in one place, in the hotel Vancouver-apparently they have to leave these premises-while the television studio, located in a former garage, is an absolute disgrace. It is amazing to me they can turn out good productions with such a poor physical plant. Since the opportunity arose for the corporation to go to the Kitsilano site there has been a long discussion among the

city council, the parks board, the federal authorities and the C.B.C. concerning this move. The latest proposal is that the C.B.C. should go to downtown Vancouver. The city council is presenting a proposal for the redevelopment of the downtown area and it wants federal assistance to buy land, clear the land and redevelop it. The council wants the C.B.C. to spend a considerable amount of money putting up a fine headquarters in downtown Vancouver. I think I have the solution to this problem, Mr. Chairman, and I hope the Postmaster General will listen carefully.
In July the reeve of Burnaby sent a wire to the C.B.C. with the authority of the council to the effect that land would be available to the corporation at a nominal cost-I presume that means $1 a year-if the corporation would locate its British Columbia headquarters in Burnaby. The officers of the corporation have not, to my knowledge, gone into this subject thoroughly. Nevertheless I think the offer should be taken seriously. Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments of the time of the committee to comment on a situation that has arisen in the Department of Transport. I am exceptionally pleased that the Acting Minister of Transport is here tonight; whether or not he is listening does not matter. I have complained in the past of the practice of granting monopoly franchises to the ground transport services at national airports such as Toronto, Dorval, Winnipeg and Vancouver and now the city of Ottawa.
On Friday last I received from the government a return airplane ticket to Toronto on the 4.55 flight. 1 want to show you some of the niceties that these monopolistic organizations can enforce upon individuals, and I wish to protest. The plane on which I was booked was to go at 4.55 p.m. I showed up at the Chateau Laurier hotel at 4.02, just 53 minutes before the plane leaves. I have always been told by T.C.A. to allow 50 minutes from the Chateau Laurier to the airport. When I arrived at the transport depot at 4.03 I was told the bus had already left for the airport and I was late. The time I was told was 4.07. The starter produced his wrist watch to show me, 4.07. I pointed to the peace tower and asked him if he paid any attention to the time on the peace tower clock. He said, "We go by my wrist watch, my friend." I 
said, "It is 4.03 and I am told by T.C.A. I am to allow 50 minutes for the transfer service."
At that moment a businessman came out of the Chateau Laurier and asked where the bus to the airport was. He was told it had gone. So I said to the starter of the Red Line that has this monopoly contract, "Here's another man that is here before 4.05 and your bus service has gone." I said to the businessman, "If you and I grab a cab together we will be able to split the $4 between us which the Red Line is trying to make out of each of us." The starter informed me that it would not cost $4 for a taxi, and I said, "I have paid it in past years."
I got into the cab with the businessman. The peace tower clock was reading 4.05 and just then another member of the house, not from this side, came swinging along with his bags. He also thought 50 minutes was all he needed to allow. I got out of the cab; I was now shilling for the Red Line. I said to this other member of parliament, "They are running this service on the wrist watch of the Red Line starter. The peace tower clock means nothing to them. Would you care to climb in with me?"
The second member of parliament got in and the three of us, two members of parliament and the businessman, rode out to the airport. The charge was $3.65. As the starter said, it would not be $4. However, normally when I am forced to ride single, I pay the taxi operator $4-35 cents for himself and $3.65 for the monopoly.
These monopoly contracts should be thrown open for public tender if they are going to continue monopoly practice, but I do not believe in the monopoly practice at all. This service should be open to every taxicab service in the city of Ottawa, and this applies to other communities across Canada.
Many of you may realize I have strong feelings on the liquor question. I am sorry that last week, in walking home up Bank street, for the first time in some years I saw a customer being ejected from a Bank street hotel. It was not any too pleasant a sight and a free-for-all fight developed on the corner. It was a little upsetting and the language was pretty vile.
I began to look for a policeman, as I often see these police cars going up and down the street, and as we always say, when you look for one there isn't one. However, in a couple of moments a police car came by. I hailed the chap and I said to him, "It is pretty rough at that ladies' entrance to the hotel one block

down the street. One chap"-I described him -"is the centre of the group, I think you should break it up." To my surprise the policeman whistled away faster than a Canada goose, and I thought to myself that this was a pretty funny thing for the Ottawa police department. I know there is a great deal of merit attached to the setting up of an advisory committee. That committee will, no doubt, come up with a report which will be of great value to parliament. However, we would like to have been able to look into some of these aspects of the corporation's affairs before being obliged to approve these large expenditures. As things stand, the areas which are not now served can more or less sit back and accept the position that nothing whatsoever is to be done with respect to providing services until this advisory committee on broadcasting reports to the government or to the corporation or to whomever they are going to report.

To be a complete service, covering in fair proportion the whole range of programming; bringing things of interest, value, and entertainment to-people of all tastes, ages, and interests, and not concentrating on some aspects of broadcasting to. the exclusion of others.
To link all parts of the country in two ways: (1) through the inclusion of a wide variety of national and common interests in its program services; (2) by using its physical resources to bring the national program service to as many Canadians as finances allow. The system of priorities outlined above has-been followed by C.B.C. for some years and is in line with the proportion of the over-all budget which it is felt can be devoted to this aspect of development. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words concerning the administration of justice.
I want to take advantage of this preliminary remark to point out that if all members could do their utmost to summarize their thoughts, to synthesize their remarks, we could save a lot of time. Some members speak at length nothing but absolute nonsense. I think we could synthesize our ideas. That is what I intend to do tonight in dealing with the matter of justice.
Mr. Chairman, the respect of justice, of the judicial institutions and of those whose duty it is to interpret and administer the law, is a categorical imperative in every well organized society.
When the reputation of justice or of those whose duty it is to administer justice, is compromised, anarchy is liable to develop.
We have been recently aware of events where the integrity of the judicature has been impaired.
One has only to remember, Mr. Chairman, the Coffin case to confine to oblivion events which it is preferable not to mention.
I believe that our judicial system ranks above that of our neighbours to the south, since in Canada, none of those exercising judiciary functions have to be elected to do so.
However, it is obvious, whether we like it or not, that since confederation the appointment of judges has too often, unfortunately, been an instrument of patronage.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that our courts, and more particularly our superior courts, should be above all reproach as far as their efficiency and integrity are concerned. That is the reason I advocate, concerning the appointment of superior court justices, a special piece of legislation which would include strict provisions and require, as an obligation, consultations with the bar association and the bench of the provinces where appointments are to be made. In my opinion, every province-and this should be done upon the initiative of the federal government-should have a committee of the bar association and a committee of high ranking judges which would look into and oversee the appointment of judges. I believe that, should this committee of the bar association and the committee of high ranking judges, whose creation I suggest and which would be advisory bodies, object to the appointment of a certain lawyer to the bench, then the minister of justice would have to consider this opposition as a

Interim Supply
right o 1 veto. This would prevent the appointment of judges who do not possess the qualifications required to fulfil their duties.
Mr. Chairman, by all means we must reestablish the prestige and integrity of the bench. There must be an end to this system of giving sole consideration to partisanship. The appointment of judges should be based on standards of competence and integrity and not solely on partisanship considerations. Let us restore the prestige of justice and the prestige of those who administer justice. We must strengthen the people's confidence in the administration of justice, a confidence which has been shaken by incidents better left unmentioned.

There is a very serious problem in regard to eastern agriculture and certainly the feed grain policy is part of that problem.
One of my main reasons for participating in the debate is that I have before me a letter I received from a farmer in my constituency. I must say immediately that the letter is not written from any political point of view. I could read the entire letter into the record but I do not think that is necessary. It is necessary, however, for me to refer to certain facts contained in it. I know this farmer very well. I know what his previous political affiliation was. I do not know whether he is still of the same mind in that regard but certainly he was not a supporter of mine. In his letter he has this to say:
I have 200 acres and am in mixed farming. First, let us look at the beef situation. I bought 50 good western steer calves last winter for 242 cents per pound, figuring I got a good buy. They cost me on an average of $145 each. After feeding them for nine months, if X sold them now

I would probably make $25 a piece. I have no choice but to stable these cattle and buy corn and concentrate and finish them and hope the price goes up. At today's prices the banker will have more money out of them than I will.
I shipped eight good shorthorn heifers this fall and the price I got ranged from 18 cents to 20 cents in Toronto. It is a long time since cattle have been below 20 cents per pound.
Let's take a look at hogs. A few years back we got between $50 and $60 per pig with hog grower at $45 per ton. Today we get around $40 per pig and pay $78 per ton for feed. Buy a pig at $12 and feed it 700 pounds of feed at that price and you see what your profit is.
Now for poultry, the real moneymakers. I keep 40 hens. We got 23 to 25 cents per dozen most of the summer for eggs. The government is giving us a deficiency payment on the three top grades of eggs, but what about the lower grades? It costs just as much to produce those small eggs as the large ones. How are you going to make a hen lay all large eggs?
I house my pullets and wanted to sell the year old hens. All I could get for these birds was 5 cents per pound. A four pound hen would bring 20 cents. With prices like this and the high cost of labour, machinery, taxes, (etc.), which you know as much about as I do, how in the world is the farmer going to exist?
Now, listen to this, Mr. Chairman:
Surely, our Minister of Agriculture and farmer members must realize this, or are they all millionaires?
We know that is not the case, of course; but it seems so to the average farmer in eastern Canada.
I hope you will present this situation to whom it may concern, and trust that something will be done before the small farmer falls by the wayside.
Now, Mr. Chairman, perhaps this does not seem very important in the course of this debate. I have here quotations that were supplied to me by the hon. member for Grey North, but before proceeding, Mr. Chairman, may I ask you to take note of the lengthy interjections during my humble intervention.
