It is not for me to say, as has been repeated so many times during the last few days, that members of parliament should not be concerned with programming. Maybe this is so. I do not believe it is quite the case, but maybe these other members are right. They may be more accurate than I in this regard, but I do say the time has come for the expenditures of the C.B.C. to be placed before parliament each and every year, the same as the expenditures of any ministry, not for the purpose of considering programming but for the purpose of considering the expenditures themselves.
We have received a large number of letters from good, sound, sensible, Canadian families. They have sent letters to their respective members of parliament, and these people are burdened with the expenditure of $100 million a year for something that they deplore. When that happens there is something wrong with our system. If that is not so, then probably I am wrong in being on the floor or occupying my seat, but I believe we should stand up for the people who object to the money the government spends through the C.B.C.
Incidentally I do not always have the opportunity to listen to all the broadcasts of the C.B.C., but I have not heard the C.B.C. say one word today about the objections that have been raised here. Do the orders for this type of attitude come from the top? I do not believe these attitudes originate below the top level. They originate with the policy people, and it is not fair enough for anyone on the other side of the chamber to reply, "You appointed these men who have the authority. Why don't they act?"
The point is that if the Canadian taxpayers have a problem surely they have the right, through their duly elected members, to place their objection before the authority concerned.

Is it any wonder we have trouble in our universities, with the movements that fly off to the left, when we are given leadership such as this and our young people can see it for what it is? speechtext: I was about to congratulate the hon. member for Grey-Bruce for having completed his remarks within the time allotted to him, without an interruption. I permitted a question. It was a long question and there was a long answer, and I think we should now call on the next speaker.

On a point of order; a few minutes ago the President of the Privy Council maintained that the estimates of the C.B.C. were not before us. On page 54 of the main estimates which were given to all members earlier in the session there is an item, vote 1, in the amount of $85,900,000. Then the first paragraph of the resolution before the committee this evening includes these words:
(a) two twelfths of the total of all of the items to be voted in the main estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1965-
Then there are some exceptions; but the C.B.C. is not included in any of those exceptions. The government is asking for two twelfths of this $85,900,000 mentioned in the main estimates; that is, if my arithmetic is correct, $14,316,000. I wonder whether the President of the Privy Council would agree that by passing this resolution we do in fact grant that much money to the C.B.C. for its operations and therefore, at least to this extent the estimates of the C.B.C. are before the committee.

If that is a question directed to me, let me say I would agree that the committee does authorize the government to make this advance, but I would also point out to the hon. member that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, were passed many

weeks ago, yet he will find a reference to them in the resolution as well.

I do not intend to make any ruling on the point of order raised by the hon. member. If it should be necessary the chairman will make a ruling upon his return. It would seem to me, however, that the discussion so far has been in order, and if I were to make a ruling that would be my ruling.

I am glad you made that ruling, Mr. Chairman. This seems to be a take-a-whack-at-the-C.B.C.-week, and I do not want to change the topic. However, I do not intend to take a whack at the C.B.C. although I think you will recognize, Mr. Chairman as most members will, that there must be something wrong with the C.B.C. to have aroused the ire of so many members of this house.
On all sides.

On some sides and in some corners of this house. After all, what can you expect when you have a body which is really not responsible to anyone? It is no more the fault of members on this side than of members on the other. I recall listening to my hon. friend from York-Humber about a month ago when he spoke about the origin of the C.B.C. and the wonderful work it had done at that time. Since those days the needs of the country have changed and the C.B.C. has changed, but because there is a lack of communication of responsibility between the C.B.C. and the shareholders, who are the people of Canada, is it any wonder that some problems arise? As to programming, I do not think anyone in this house would venture to say that he would take the responsibility for programming although, like everyone here, I like to see whether I am getting my money's worth.
During the dinner hour I went through the weekly programs of Toronto television stations. Members may recall we have channel six, which is the C.B.C.; then we have two others, nine and eleven, one of which is in Hamilton. They are private stations. I averaged out the private stations, the two of them, and the C.B.C. station and I more or less designated the programs into certain areas such as drama, variety, public affairs, and so on and we find that at the end of the week the C.B.C. did provide two hours more of drama than went out from the other stations, or the average of both of them; it provided three and a half hours more of imported programs such as Beverly Hillbillies and so on. It put out another three and a
Interim Supply
half hours extra of local variety programs, another nine and a half hours of sport programs, an extra four hours of public affairs, and three extra hours of educational programs. And that is what the corporation has done. I doubt the value of the imported programs.
The question which comes to my mind is: Is that worth $1,500,000? Is it worth as much money as we are paying out-roughly $2 million a week? Granted, all these programs are very good, very beneficial-drama, education, and so on. But is it worth $2 million? For this reason I cannot see anything wrong with either a committee or any other body studying the whole concept of the C.B.C.
Is it still in the interest of the nation to have the C.B.C. decide by itself what is to be the cultural destiny of this nation? Are they fulfilling the function they are supposed to fulfil? Can it not be done by private television? Could it be possible that the C.B.C. should not be in competitive television, or in the business of trying to make money at television? All these questions could be decided by either such a committee, or a very deep study as to what terms of reference we are going to give the C.B.C. from now on. It is not enough to stand up in this house and say, "The C.B.C. did such and such. The program was wrong. We want to control this," or, "we want to control that". I believe we have to go deeper; we have to find out what is the future of public broadcasting. Is it still necessary? How much of it is necessary? In what direction will it go? I believe this should be a subject of detailed study by a committee and I urge the government to take into consideration the requests that have been made for the seting up of a committee to study the whole problem of the C.B.C., or public broadcasting in its entirety.

Mr. Chairman, there has been considerable discussion of the C.B.C. during the past two days. Most hon. members have been critical of this crown corporation. However, a great deal of the criticism has been constructive and justifiable. Especially has this been true of the remarks today of the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for Churchill. There are also many others who are appreciative of the work of this important national service.
I think it is interesting to recall the early stages or the beginnings of television in Canada. A late prime minister, R. B. Bennett, said in this House of Commons in 1932:
This country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian

Interim Supply
sources, free from foreign interference or influence, No other system than that of public ownership can ensure to the people of this country without regard to class or place, equal enjoyment of the benefits and pleasures of radio broadcasting.
The Liberal opposition wholly endorsed this view and the act of 1932 was adopted without a single dissenting voice. Throughout the years this great national service has developed in many directions. As we examine the C.B.C. we should in fairness remind ourselves of its admitted achievements. I wish to summarize briefly five areas of interest and accomplishment.
1.	Both radio and television programs are presented daily to Canadian listeners and viewers in both English and French.
2.	A great variety of attractions is provided, from popular sports and entertainment to public affairs and grand opera. The high standard of these programs is recognized annually by C.B.C.'s success in receiving an impressive series of awards in competition with American networks.
3.	The C.B.C. provides a rare opportunity for the training and employment of musicians, artists, writers and commentators; not just a few in Toronto and Montreal but approximately 20,000 across Canada at the many production points. In one year approximately $16 million is paid to these talented people.
4.	The C.B.C. helped to create Canada's image to the world by operating the international service; broadcasting by radio to a hundred countries in a dozen languages. Program offices are maintained in London, Paris and New York.
5.	Free time on radio and television has been allocated to all political parties during and between election campaigns. This policy of using public funds to prepare the electorate for voting day has been widely appreciated.
Over the past 30 years there have been three royal commissions and 14 parliamentary committees which have all been charged with the responsibility of having a good look at the C.B.C. Each of these commissions and committees has arrived at the same conclusion; that Canadians want a national broadcasting service and they want it to be of a high standard. The most recent examination of the administration was made by the Fowler commission in 1957, which concluded its report with these words:
We must be prepared to spend public money in quite large quantities. The Canadian economy is just not big enough to support a broadcasting system on commercial resources alone. At least it would not be one we would want to have or one that would be anything more than the

scattered outposts of American networks. The central factor in a Canadian system is the C.B.C. supported by money out of the public treasury for both its capital and operating needs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend
to offer any vigorous criticism of the C.B.C. tonight, except to offer a word of caution to them. I think they must have recognized by now that the people of Canada are in fact alarmed about some of their programs. I am not one who has been too disappointed with the C.B.C. I think some of their programs are excellent; they compare very favourably with any t.v. programs in our modern western world. But I think the least they could do would be to give warning and state that these controversial subjects are going to be broadcast, so that at least those parents who have any control over the television in their homes-and most of us still have some-could encourage their children to look at something else.
I think some of these programs are educational and the motives behind putting them on are not pornographic or even to be very sensational. However, Mr. Chairman, I believe some care should be taken to make sure they are screened to the extent that they are not suddenly forced upon us in the middle of family viewing. If this is beyond the intelligence of the C.B.C. perhaps we will have to institute some form of screening. I am afraid of anything approaching government interference in this regard; in fact my main complaint about the C.B.C. is the fact that in our efforts to put them above interference we have made it possible for some people to use this medium as a very definite channel of political propaganda. 1 do not use the word "propaganda" accidentally, because I think it is an abuse of our privileges and freedoms when a member of any party can get on the air and give very, very controversial views and ideas, unless there is at least some balance, some opportunity for opposition to it if another party wishes to refute it at the time it should be refuted, which is right away. If you get on the air and give a lengthy statement on any subject, you can never withdraw it; it has gone out to the four corners of the country and it is impossible to undo the damage by merely saying a day or two later that you did not mean it, or something like that.

If on the particular program itself-and we have had some very good arguments brought before the public-views are expressed by all parties through representatives on the program, I think this is educational and should not be stopped. But the idea of using the air waves, especially at the expense of the taxpayer, to brainwash people is an abuse of our freedom which I for one am certainly dead against. That is my main criticism of the actual programming of the C.B.C.
I have another complaint to make. I do not think it is fair to spend all the taxpayers' money in one particular city. If we construct buildings in Montreal or Toronto costing $45 or $60 million it is going to be hard to sell the idea to the people living in sparsely populated areas that we are not putting all our eggs in one basket. As I said before I think C.B.C. programs are good but there are still many people in Canada not receiving them.
Therefore I should like to see the C.B.C. budget their expenditures, first of all to try to provide coverage to everyone in Canada before we go into the super luxury field. I think that $45 million or $60 million spent on one building is providing perhaps a little too much luxury for us at this particular stage. I am only giving an amateur's opinion of course; but the people in my sparsely populated district are not adequately covered by the C.B.C.
In view of the fact we are on interim supply I should like at this point to make a general complaint. I do not think that the members of this house are consulted enough in matters affecting their own ridings. If in the past governments have refused to consult with members of parliament this is a mistake, and let us not duplicate the mistakes of the past. For example, at the present time western Canada is largely represented in this house by the members of one party. Are we to ignore forever the needs of the people in the rural areas of western Canada merely because they are represented by only one party? To say that that is the way R. B. Bennett or Mackenzie King did it is not good enough for 1964.
We are being criticized both in the press and on television for not doing our job. If that is true it is because we are not keeping up with the problems of the day, problems which are new. We require greater co-operation and the government in power, particularly when it is a minority government, should be only too pleased to ask our opinion 20220-602
Interim Supply
on matters. We cannot force them to do this but we do represent a cross section of the people; and as the present government only represents only one third of the constituencies in Canada surely something would be gained from consultation.
Some hon. members have suggested changing our committees system. We are now in committee of the whole, and I would suggest to this government that they or any other government which might take over might well use the intelligence and well thought out planning of other party members to enrich the life of our nation.
In the northern part of Alberta the C.B.C. are trying to set up booster stations to supply some television coverage, following along the line I have suggested of providing more coverage for our people before spending most of our money in one particular area. The rumour I have heard-it is only a rumour; I have had no official notice of this-is that a booster station will be erected at Slave Lake, northern Alberta. There is already a good booster station at Grande Prairie. This will cause overlapping of service, with double coverage in the Peace River area in the west end of my district and very little coverage in the central or eastern part. In cases like this a little consultation might have helped. If this station were constructed in the town of Athabasca rather than Slave Lake twice the area would be covered. The areas already covered would not suffer at all and television service would be provided to another 20,000 people who need it badly. It is probably the only television station they can tune into. I submit this is a fair way to spend some money; it is using it wisely and spending it where it will do the most good.
Not only in C.B.C. matters but also on agricultural questions and in other departments I think hon. gentlemen opposite could well use the information and the local knowledge which we have and which we are only too willing to give. I would even suggest that the government should not be allowed to spend more than $5,000 in any hon. member's constituency without first warning that hon. member. Then if he is not to be in any way affected by the administration of that money he should certainly have the right to say what he knows about the local conditions, and an alert government would be glad to hear it.
I have mentioned this before in matters affecting the post office. I do not think that anyone would want to deny people the proper delivery of Her Majesty's mails, yet during the

Interim Supply
last 18 months I have never been consulted on the postal requirements in my district in any shape or form. I am not at all satisfied with the excuse that R. B. Bennett did not do it so this government will not do it. If that sort of thing took place there would be no progress whatever. This same reply has been given on more than one occasion. It is said that ministers 20 years ago did not answer questions so these ministers are not answering them.
This gives credence to the criticisms we are getting. I would warn the Liberal party that this sort of criticism usually comes from the longhairs or splinter parties. I think it would be a good idea if we smartened up and gave the kind of leadership which the two old parties are better qualified to give.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Too late.
Ten o'clock.

You can tell from the heckling, Mr. Chairman, that I am drawing some blood down there in the corner. They know what I am saying is true. There is a long and arduous campaign to discredit the older parties so as to assist one particular group of members in the house, and we all know who they are. They are members who never make a positive contribution themselves.
Ten o'clock.

The handout programs are always their remedy because they do not have to raise the money. It is easy to ride the white horse when you do not have responsibility. In the six years I have been here I have never heard these people make any suggestions concerning how to raise more money. Their free money or give-away programs will never accomplish this. May I call it ten o'clock?
Progress reported.
I should like to ask the acting house leader whether the government intends to continue tomorrow the discussion on interim supply.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. Tomorrow we will continue this discussion of interim supply, and when that is completed we will take up main estimates, departments of citizenship and immigration, forestry and national revenue.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
